title: Seed Dispersal Designs
question: How does wing area affect model-seed landing distance when mass, release height and the fan setting are kept the same?

blocks.prompt: Required before releases: Which wing design do you predict will have the greater mean (average) landing distance at your chosen fan setting? Explain why one release might not settle the question.
blocks.text: The larger effective wing may have a greater mean distance, but releases may vary and overlap.

blocks.prompt: Required before releases: Why keep total mass and release height the same? How will repeated releases help you distinguish a design difference from variation between drops?
blocks.text: Keep total mass, release height and nominal wind the same. Compare three separate releases per design and their means and ranges.
Timing: Before balance or flight observations.
Chosen nominal wind: 1 m/s. Release height: 2.0 m. Both total model masses: 0.20 g. These are supplied model settings.

The small wing has an effective area of 10 cm² and the large wing 20 cm². Both supplied models have a total mass of 0.20 g, including their bodies and matched ballast, or added weight. Verify both on the model balance. Release from 2.0 m with the same nominal fan setting. Modeled gusts and small differences in drag create variation between releases.

Distances refer to first ground contact from the vertical release line, read to 0.1 m. Airtime is model-computed, not timed by the student. Each row is a separate synthetic release; no field measurements or independent plants are claimed.

blocks.prompt: Describe the design difference and the controls you verified. How can air resistance and time in the air affect sideways movement? Why is this a model rather than a complete simulation of a maple seed?
blocks.text: My controls explanation uses actual distances 0.7, 1, 0.9 m for the small wing and 1.5, 2.1, 1.9 m for the large wing. Both masses were supplied as 0.20 g, with the same height and nominal wind. Separate drops vary, so means and ranges add context to one landing. I read the first distance for each design, and four later readings were model-provided. This drag-based paper model omits real maple rotation and lift. Distance alone does not measure habitat quality, survival or fitness.

blocks.prompt: Why keep total mass the same when comparing the two wing areas?
blocks.text:
Changing mass too could change the flight, making the wing-area comparison harder to interpret.
Correct! Mass and the way air acts on a design both affect its motion. Matching mass, release height and nominal wind helps focus this model comparison on area. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: What do the three releases per design help show?
blocks.text:
Variation in the synthetic releases, so a mean and range add context to a single landing.
Correct! Each release has a separate modeled gust/drag variation. The mean summarizes the set; the range is largest minus smallest. Three synthetic releases are not a large field study. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: Which conclusion goes beyond the evidence collected?
blocks.text:
The farther-traveling design must always leave more surviving offspring in nature.
Correct! Distance is one part of dispersal. Landing habitat, germination, competition and survival also matter. The model did not measure reproduction or natural selection. Revised after feedback.

These are artificial teaching designs and synthetic flight data, not measured seeds or calibrated fan experiments. Mass, effective area, release height and air settings are supplied model quantities. The balance displays the supplied total mass. A simple two-dimensional gravity and air-resistance calculation uses assumed drag properties, with seeded gust/drag variation. It does not simulate realistic wing rotation, lift, swirling air around rotating wings, canopy collisions or complex turbulence. The flight drawing and timing are illustrative; seed symbols are enlarged. A landing is the first ground contact, with no bouncing or rolling. Three releases show model variation but do not establish a reliable difference in real field conditions. Greater distance alone does not prove better survival or evolutionary fitness. No physical fan/drop protocol is supplied.
